# @tduyng/pi-opencode-z

opencode's Zen models in pi, free ones included, with no API key and no proxy. The bridge drives the opencode server already running on the machine.

Since September 2026 the free tier answers any direct API call with `403 FreeTierError: "OpenCode's free tier can only be used from within OpenCode"`. No key and no proxy gets around it, because the check is on where the request originates.

So the extension does not call the Zen API. It drives the opencode background server and lets opencode make the upstream call, which is the one thing the free tier accepts.

## The conversation lives in opencode

The bridge sends only the new message each turn instead of re-serialising the transcript, and the tool schemas sit in opencode's cached prefix rather than being pasted back as prose on every request.

The bridge exposes pi's tools over MCP as `pi_read`, `pi_bash`, `pi_edit` and so on. When the model calls one, the bridge holds that MCP request open, hands the call to pi, and pi runs the real tool against the real project. The answer goes back over the same held request and opencode carries on in the same session. The model never touches files directly.

Nothing is written to the repository. Each pi session gets one opencode session rooted in a throwaway temp directory holding its `opencode.jsonc`, and `~/.config/opencode` is untouched.

A mode switch that adds or removes tools keeps the session too: the bridge pushes `notifications/tools/list_changed` over MCP, opencode re-lists, and the cached prefix survives.

## The token floor

A plain `opencode run` on a free model spends 9,176 input tokens on a one-line prompt. This bridge spends 6,941, with 2,048 of those served from cache. That floor is opencode's own system prompt and built-in tool schemas, and every approach pays it, because stripping those tools is exactly what trips the 403.

What the bridge saves is per turn. A full tool-calling turn with a real file read takes about 10 seconds end to end.

## Use

Run `/model` and pick anything under the `opencode-z` provider, for example `opencode-z/mimo-v2.6-flash-free`.

```text
pi --provider opencode-z --model mimo-v2.6-flash-free
```

| Command | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `/opencode-z status` | Server url, config file, models filter, MCP endpoint, live sessions, model list |
| `/opencode-z models` | The models alone, free ones first |
| `/opencode-z refresh` | Re-read the config and the catalogue without restarting pi |
| `/opencode-z config` | Resolved settings and where they come from |
| `/opencode-z help` | Usage |

## Install

- The `opencode` CLI on `PATH`, or `OPENCODE_Z_BIN` pointing at it.
- The opencode background server. If it is not running, the bridge runs `opencode service start`.
- No API key and no account.

```bash
pi install npm:@tduyng/pi-opencode-z
```

The bridge reads the server url and password from `~/.local/state/opencode/service.json` and talks to it over HTTP basic auth as user `opencode`.

Settings live in `~/.pi/agent/pi-opencode-z.json`, and a project's `.pi/pi-opencode-z.json` overrides it field by field. Environment variables override both, so a one-off run never needs a file.

Free models only:

```json
{
  "models": "free"
}
```

A pinned list with a custom binary:

```json
{
  "bin": "/path/to/opencode",
  "models": ["mimo-v2.6-flash-free", "muse-spark-1.3"]
}
```

`models` narrows what gets registered: `free` keeps zero-cost models, and a comma-separated string or an array pins the list. Unset or empty, every Zen model the account can reach is registered. Only Zen models appear, never other providers. `OPENCODE_Z_BIN` and `OPENCODE_Z_MODELS` do the same per process and win over the file.

It adds no tool, no prompt block and no schema, so the context is pi's own and cold start is unchanged.

## Notes

The bridge never denies opencode's built-in tools. A `deny` rule anywhere in the agent's permissions trips the free-tier 403 even for allowed tools, so every action stays on `ask` and the bridge rejects the unwanted ones at runtime. A weaker model sometimes reaches for its built-in `read` first, gets refused, and retries with `pi_read`, which costs one round trip.

opencode adds and retires Zen models often, so the bridge reads the catalogue live at startup and `/opencode-z refresh` re-reads it.

The first prompt lists the exact MCP names available in that turn. Some model hosts display these tools under a `functions.` namespace, and the bridge states that the label does not rename a tool, so a model does not mistake a disabled `read` for `pi_read`.

opencode stops a whole step when the model calls two built-in tools at once, since refusing one declines the rest. The bridge counts its own refusals and, when that stop was its doing, re-prompts the same session with a nudge back to the `pi_` tools, at most twice per turn.

When a turn fails, the bridge interrupts opencode and answers waiting tool calls with an error. It keeps the opencode session when pi's transcript still ends at the last completed user message, so a retry reuses the prompt cache, and drops it when a partial assistant or tool result is present.

## Sleep and wake

macOS freezes every process on sleep, but a wall-clock timer keeps counting, so a 300 second deadline spent overnight fires the moment the lid opens. Deadlines here are measured in awake time instead. A suspended machine spends none of the budget, and the same holds for the 15 second API request and the 4 second service probe.

A turn that died during a sleep is retried once on the same opencode session, as long as the model had not produced text or a tool call yet. The upstream connection to Zen is what broke, not the conversation. After a wake the bridge also re-checks opencode's MCP link, because opencode gives up reconnecting after two attempts. A dead link rebuilds the opencode session, which connects again.

herdr keeps the pi process alive across a detach. It does not keep pi's sockets alive across a sleep, and the above covers that case.

## Limits

- A turn that makes no progress for 300 awake seconds is interrupted, and an MCP exec times out at 300 seconds. Streaming text, reasoning or a tool call counts as progress, so a slow model that keeps talking is not cut off. A timeout usually means the model was still working.
- The API request times out at 15 awake seconds, and the MCP body is capped at 8 MB.
- A step that produces reasoning but no text and no tool call is re-prompted through a bounded recovery path, twice per turn at most.
- Free-tier model availability is opencode's to change. The list is read live for that reason.
